newsitem.title: UK: Scientists intrigued by CJD blood finding.
newsitem.headline: Scientists intrigued by CJD blood finding.

text.p: British scientists said on Thursday they were intrigued but not worried by a report that the human version of mad cow disease could possibly be passed on in blood.

After hearing the report and comments by scientists, the World Health Organisation said it would issue recommendations that certain people at possible risk of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) should not donate blood.
Dr Paul Brown of the U.S. National Institutes of Health told reporters in Geneva on Wednesday that tests with mice indicated that CJD could possibly be transmitted in blood.

He injected blood from mice infected with human CJD into the brains of healthy mice. The healthy mice became ill, he said. He did not say whether he had conducted the necessary brain biopsy to see whether the injected mice actually had CJD.
He told a news conference the risk of blood plasma passing on CJD was small, but still existed. Brown's findings have not been published and several British experts declined comment.
A British health ministry spokesman said the government was not worried. "My understanding is that this experiment involved injecting blood directly into the brain of a mouse," he said.
"That is a procedure which would never be carried out on a human being anyway. We regard it as a purely experimental procedure that has no basis in medical science."
Sheila Gore, a Medical Research Council expert on CJD and mad cow disease in Cambridge, called Brown's report very interesting.

"It's what some people would expect," she said, noting that the molecular marker -- a type of chemical flag -- for bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease) had been found in tonsils. "That brought concern that the agent was in lymph sites and therefore in blood," she added.

Scientists believe BSE and CJD are caused by mutated prions, brain proteins that seem to have the ability to replicate themselves. Evidence of infectious prions has been found in various organs of infected animals, including the brain, spinal cord and small intestines, but not the blood.

A new variant of CJD was identified last year, affecting younger people than usual. Scientists said it was probably caused by eating BSE-infected beef. Fifteen victims -- one French and the rest British -- have been confirmed.
The WHO recommended that people who received human growth hormones in the early 1980s should not donate blood.
A few such people have died from CJD. The hormones were taken from the pituitary glands in the brains of corpses, some of which evidently had the deadly brain-wasting CJD.
Once the danger was discovered, the use of human hormones was discontinued. Artificial hormones are now used.

The families of eight British victims are suing the health ministry and the Medical Research Council (MRC), a government body, on the grounds that scientists continued the treatments after they should have known of the risks.
WHO also recommended that people related to someone who died of CJD not donate blood, as there is known to be a genetic component to the one-in-a-million disease.
It also named a third group -- people who received a transplant of dura mater, the outermost covering of the brain. It is used in neurosurgery and some other surgical techniques.
Britain's National Blood Transfusion Service already excludes the first two groups from donating.
A spokeswoman said the agency was working on finding a viable way to exclude the third group. "It is likely to be a very small number of people," she said.
